questions.stem:
(a) List five characteristics that are common to all living organisms. [5 marks]
(b) A motor car takes in fuel and air, moves, gives out exhaust gases and produces heat. Explain three reasons why it is NOT regarded as a living thing. [6 marks]
(c) (i) What is irritability? (ii) Give one example of irritability in a named plant and one in a named animal. [4 marks]
(d) State five differences between a green plant and a mammal. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) Any five, 1 mark each: nutrition; respiration; excretion; growth; reproduction; irritability/sensitivity; movement
6 marks: (b) Any three explained, 2 marks each: cannot reproduce its own kind; does not grow by adding new protoplasm/cells; does not respond to stimuli on its own; is not made of cells/protoplasm; fuel is burnt, not respired by cells
2 marks: (c)(i) The ability of a living organism to detect and respond to changes (stimuli) in its environment
2 marks: (c)(ii) Plant: e.g. Mimosa leaflets fold when touched / shoot bends towards light (1 mark); animal: e.g. withdrawal of hand from hot object / earthworm moves away from light (1 mark)
5 marks: (d) Any five contrasts, 1 mark each: plant makes own food, mammal feeds on ready-made food; plant cells have cellulose walls, mammal cells do not; plant has chlorophyll, mammal has none; plant growth localised at tips, mammal grows all over; plant does not move from place to place, mammal moves; plant has no specialised excretory organ, mammal has kidneys; plant responds slowly, mammal responds quickly via nerves
questions.explanation: Living things feed, respire, excrete, grow, reproduce, respond and move. A car is not alive because it cannot reproduce, does not grow from within, is not cellular and does not respond to stimuli by itself. Irritability is sensitivity to stimuli, e.g. Mimosa folding on touch or a lizard running from a predator. Plants are autotrophic, have cellulose walls and chlorophyll and localised growth; mammals are heterotrophic, mobile and have nervous and excretory systems.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between sexual and asexual reproduction. [4 marks]
(b) Describe binary fission in Amoeba. [6 marks]
(c) Name one organism that reproduces by each of the following methods: (i) budding; (ii) fragmentation; (iii) spore formation; (iv) vegetative propagation by stem tubers. [4 marks]
(d) State three advantages and three disadvantages of asexual reproduction to a population. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Sexual: involves two parents / fusion of gametes (fertilisation); offspring show variation
2 marks: (a) Asexual: one parent; no fusion of gametes; offspring identical to parent (clones)
1 mark: (b) Amoeba grows to full size and stops feeding/becomes rounded
2 marks: (b) The nucleus divides into two (by mitosis), the daughter nuclei move apart
2 marks: (b) The cytoplasm constricts in the middle and divides
1 mark: (b) Two daughter amoebae are formed, each grows to adult size
4 marks: (c) 1 mark each: (i) yeast / Hydra; (ii) Spirogyra; (iii) Rhizopus / Mucor / fern / mushroom; (iv) Irish potato / yam
3 marks: (d) Advantages, any three, 1 mark each: rapid; only one parent needed; good traits preserved; offspring can quickly colonise a favourable area
3 marks: (d) Disadvantages, any three, 1 mark each: no variation; all offspring equally susceptible to disease; overcrowding and competition near parent; little adaptation to changing environment
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction involves fusion of gametes from two parents and gives variation; asexual reproduction involves one parent and identical offspring. In binary fission Amoeba becomes rounded, its nucleus divides by mitosis and the cytoplasm constricts to give two daughter cells. Examples: yeast (budding), Spirogyra (fragmentation), Rhizopus (spores), Irish potato (stem tubers). Asexual reproduction is fast and needs one parent but produces no variation, so a whole population may be wiped out by one disease.

questions.stem:
(a) Name three supporting tissues in flowering plants. [3 marks]
(b) For each tissue named in (a), state (i) one feature of its cells; (ii) where it is found in the plant. [6 marks]
(c) Explain how a non-woody plant such as a young Amaranthus stem is kept upright. [4 marks]
(d) Explain why a freshly cut Amaranthus shoot wilts on a hot afternoon. [3 marks]
(e) State four functions of supporting tissues in plants. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Parenchyma; collenchyma; sclerenchyma (xylem accepted for one), 1 mark each
3 marks: (b)(i) Parenchyma: thin-walled, living, turgid cells; collenchyma: living cells with cellulose thickening at corners; sclerenchyma: dead cells with walls thickened with lignin (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b)(ii) Parenchyma: cortex/pith; collenchyma: just beneath the epidermis of young stems/leaf midribs; sclerenchyma: fibres in vascular bundles/pericycle, seed coats (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Cells of the cortex and pith absorb water by osmosis and become turgid, pressing against one another
2 marks: (c) Collenchyma under the epidermis gives flexible strength; the turgid tissues keep the stem firm and erect
3 marks: (d) Water lost by transpiration is not replaced because the shoot is cut off from its roots/water supply; cells lose turgor (become flaccid); the stem and leaves droop
4 marks: (e) Any four, 1 mark each: hold the plant upright; expose leaves to light; hold flowers up for pollination; resist wind/bending; support fruits; conduct water (xylem) while supporting
questions.explanation: Parenchyma (thin-walled living cells in cortex and pith), collenchyma (cells thickened at corners, beneath the epidermis) and sclerenchyma (dead lignified fibres and sclereids) support plants. Herbaceous stems depend on turgor in parenchyma plus collenchyma. A cut shoot wilts because water lost through transpiration is not replaced, so cells become flaccid. Supporting tissues hold leaves to the light, flowers for pollinators and resist wind.

questions.topic: Movement of water to the apex of trees and herbs
questions.stem:
(a) Describe the path taken by water from the soil to the leaves of a tall mango tree. [8 marks]
(b) Explain how each of the following helps the upward movement of water: (i) transpiration pull; (ii) cohesion and adhesion; (iii) root pressure; (iv) capillarity. [8 marks]
(c) Describe a simple experiment to show that water moves up a plant through the xylem. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Water enters root hairs from the soil by osmosis
2 marks: (a) Passes from cell to cell across the cortex (by osmosis/along cell walls) to the endodermis
2 marks: (a) Enters the xylem of the root, rises in xylem vessels/tracheids of the stem
2 marks: (a) Passes into xylem of the leaf veins, then to mesophyll cells, evaporates into air spaces and diffuses out through stomata
2 marks: (b)(i) Evaporation of water from leaves creates a tension/suction that pulls the water column upwards
2 marks: (b)(ii) Cohesion: water molecules attract one another, keeping the column continuous; adhesion: water molecules cling to the xylem walls, preventing the column from slipping down
2 marks: (b)(iii) Root cells actively pump ions into the xylem, water follows by osmosis, creating a pressure that pushes water up a short distance
2 marks: (b)(iv) Water rises in the narrow xylem vessels by capillary action because of their small diameter
2 marks: (c) Place the cut end of a leafy Balsam/Commelina shoot in water containing eosin/red ink for some hours
2 marks: (c) Cut a transverse section of the stem; only the xylem (vascular bundles) is stained red, showing water moves in the xylem
questions.explanation: Water enters root hairs by osmosis, crosses the cortex and endodermis into root xylem, rises through stem xylem and passes to leaf mesophyll, from which it evaporates out of the stomata. Transpiration pull creates tension; cohesion keeps the column unbroken and adhesion holds it to vessel walls; root pressure pushes from below; capillarity helps in narrow vessels. Placing a shoot in eosin and cutting sections shows that only xylem is stained.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the respiratory organ of each of the following: (i) Tilapia; (ii) grasshopper; (iii) toad (adult, on land); (iv) earthworm. [4 marks]
(b) Describe how a bony fish obtains oxygen from the water in which it lives. [8 marks]
(c) State four features common to all respiratory surfaces. [4 marks]
(d) Explain why insects can survive with no blood pigment to carry oxygen. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) 1 mark each: (i) gills; (ii) tracheal system/spiracles and tracheae; (iii) lungs (and skin/buccal cavity); (iv) moist skin/body surface
2 marks: (b) Mouth opens, floor of the buccal cavity is lowered and opercula close, so water enters the mouth
2 marks: (b) Mouth closes, floor of the buccal cavity rises, forcing water over the gills; opercula open and water leaves
2 marks: (b) Water passes over the many thin gill filaments richly supplied with blood capillaries
2 marks: (b) Oxygen dissolved in the water diffuses into the blood, carbon dioxide diffuses out; blood and water flow in opposite directions (counter-current) for efficiency
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: large surface area; thin; moist; richly supplied with blood vessels (except insects); permeable to gases
2 marks: (d) Air is carried directly to the tissues through spiracles, tracheae and fine tracheoles
2 marks: (d) Oxygen diffuses from the tracheoles straight into the cells, so blood is not needed to transport oxygen
questions.explanation: Tilapia uses gills, a grasshopper its tracheal system, an adult toad its lungs (and skin), and the earthworm its moist skin. In a fish, water is drawn into the mouth and forced over gill filaments where oxygen diffuses into blood, then out under the opercula. Respiratory surfaces are large, thin, moist and well supplied with blood. Insects deliver air directly to cells through tracheoles, so their blood does not carry oxygen.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the position of the liver in the human body and name the two blood vessels that bring blood to it. [4 marks]
(b) Explain how the liver is involved in each of the following: (i) deamination; (ii) regulation of blood sugar; (iii) detoxification; (iv) production of bile; (v) production of heat. [10 marks]
(c) State three other functions of the liver. [3 marks]
(d) Name one disease of the liver and state one cause of it. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Below the diaphragm, on the right side of the upper abdomen, partly covering the stomach
2 marks: (a) Hepatic artery; hepatic portal vein (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Excess amino acids have their amino group removed; ammonia formed is converted to urea which is carried to the kidneys
2 marks: (b)(ii) Excess glucose converted to glycogen (under insulin) and stored; glycogen converted back to glucose when blood sugar falls (glucagon)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Harmful substances such as alcohol and drugs are broken down/converted into harmless substances
2 marks: (b)(iv) Bile is made from breakdown of old red blood cells (bile pigments) and stored in the gall bladder; it emulsifies fats
2 marks: (b)(v) Its many chemical reactions release heat which is distributed by the blood to keep the body warm
3 marks: (c) Any three, 1 mark each: storage of iron/vitamins A, D, B12; formation of plasma proteins (fibrinogen, prothrombin, albumin); breakdown of old red cells; formation of red cells in the foetus; storage of blood; conversion of fats
1 mark: (d) Named disease, e.g. hepatitis / cirrhosis / liver cancer / jaundice
2 marks: (d) Correct cause, e.g. hepatitis B virus; excessive alcohol; aflatoxin in mouldy food
questions.explanation: The liver lies under the diaphragm on the right, supplied by the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein. It deaminates excess amino acids to urea, stores glucose as glycogen and releases it when needed, detoxifies alcohol and drugs, makes bile from broken-down red cells, and generates heat. It also stores iron and vitamins and makes plasma proteins. Hepatitis B (a virus) and cirrhosis (alcohol) are liver diseases.

questions.stem:
(a) What is homeostasis? [2 marks]
(b) Name six structures found in the dermis of mammalian skin. [6 marks]
(c) Explain how the skin helps to keep the body temperature of a man constant when (i) the surrounding air is very hot; (ii) the surrounding air is very cold. [8 marks]
(d) State four other functions of the skin. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The maintenance of a constant internal environment (e.g. temperature, water, sugar levels) of the body
6 marks: (b) Any six, 1 mark each: sweat gland; sweat duct; hair follicle/hair; sebaceous gland; blood capillaries/arterioles; nerve endings/sense receptors; erector (hair) muscle; fat cells (subcutaneous)
2 marks: (c)(i) Sweat glands produce more sweat; evaporation of sweat removes latent heat from the body
2 marks: (c)(i) Arterioles in the skin dilate (vasodilation); more blood flows near the surface and heat is lost by radiation
2 marks: (c)(ii) Arterioles constrict (vasoconstriction); less blood flows to the surface, so less heat is lost; sweating is reduced
2 marks: (c)(ii) Hair muscles contract, hairs stand up trapping air (insulation); shivering of muscles produces heat
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: protection against germs; prevents water loss; sense organ for touch, pain, heat; excretion of water and salts; makes vitamin D in sunlight; stores fat
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the keeping of a steady internal environment. The dermis contains sweat glands, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, blood vessels, nerve endings and erector muscles. In heat, sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss; in cold, vasoconstriction, raised hairs and shivering conserve and generate heat. The skin also protects, prevents water loss, senses stimuli, excretes and makes vitamin D.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a reflex action? [2 marks]
(b) Describe the pathway of the impulse when a barefooted boy steps on a sharp thorn and quickly lifts his foot. [8 marks]
(c) Give four differences between a reflex action and a voluntary action. [4 marks]
(d) (i) What is a conditioned reflex? (ii) Give one example from everyday life. [3 marks]
(e) State three ways in which reflex actions are useful to an animal. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought (controlled by the spinal cord)
2 marks: (b) Pain receptors in the skin of the foot are stimulated and produce an impulse
2 marks: (b) The impulse travels along a sensory neurone through the dorsal root into the spinal cord
2 marks: (b) In the grey matter it passes across a synapse to a relay neurone, then to a motor neurone
2 marks: (b) The motor neurone carries the impulse through the ventral root to the leg muscles (effector), which contract to lift the foot
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: reflex is automatic, voluntary is deliberate; reflex is fast, voluntary slower; reflex mainly via spinal cord, voluntary controlled by the cerebrum; reflex is inborn, voluntary is learned/willed; reflex response same each time, voluntary may vary
1 mark: (d)(i) A reflex acquired through learning/association, in which a response is produced by a stimulus not normally linked to it
2 marks: (d)(ii) Any correct example, e.g. mouth watering at the sight/smell of food, pupils rising when the school bell rings
3 marks: (e) Any three, 1 mark each: protects from injury; quick escape from danger; keeps body processes going without thought (breathing, blinking); maintains balance/posture; frees the brain for other activities
questions.explanation: A reflex is a rapid automatic response. A thorn stimulates pain receptors; the impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord, via a relay neurone to a motor neurone and on to leg muscles that lift the foot. Reflexes are automatic, fast, inborn and spinal; voluntary actions are deliberate, slower and controlled by the cerebrum. A conditioned reflex is learned by association, e.g. salivating at a familiar dinner bell. Reflexes protect the body and keep vital processes going.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the three regions of the mammalian ear and two structures found in each region. [9 marks]
(b) Describe how a person hears the sound of a drum beaten nearby. [7 marks]
(c) State two ways by which the ear may be damaged and one way of caring for the ear. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Outer ear: pinna, external auditory canal (meatus), eardrum accepted (1 mark region + structures)
3 marks: (a) Middle ear: ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), Eustachian tube, oval window
3 marks: (a) Inner ear: cochlea, semicircular canals, utriculus/sacculus, auditory nerve
1 mark: (b) Sound waves are collected by the pinna and directed along the auditory canal
1 mark: (b) Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate
2 marks: (b) Vibrations are transmitted and amplified by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) to the oval window
1 mark: (b) Vibration of the oval window sets up waves in the fluid (perilymph/endolymph) of the cochlea
1 mark: (b) Sensory hair cells in the cochlea are stimulated to produce impulses
1 mark: (b) Impulses pass along the auditory nerve to the brain (cerebrum) where they are interpreted as sound
2 marks: (c) Any two, 1 mark each: very loud noise; inserting sharp objects; infection of the middle ear; a blow to the ear
2 marks: (c) Any one care measure, 2 marks: avoid loud noise / use ear protection; do not insert sharp objects; seek treatment for ear infections; clean only the outer ear
questions.explanation: The outer ear (pinna, canal), middle ear (ossicles, Eustachian tube) and inner ear (cochlea, semicircular canals) work together. Sound is funnelled to the eardrum, amplified by the ossicles to the oval window, sets cochlear fluid moving and stimulates hair cells; the auditory nerve carries impulses to the cerebrum. Loud noise, sharp objects and infection damage the ear; avoiding these protects hearing.

questions.stem:
(a) What is metamorphosis? [2 marks]
(b) Distinguish between complete and incomplete metamorphosis, naming one insect showing each type. [6 marks]
(c) Describe the life history of the butterfly from egg to adult. [8 marks]
(d) State two ways in which the larva of a butterfly is of economic importance to a farmer, and one way of controlling it. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The series of changes in form/structure an insect goes through from egg to adult
2 marks: (b) Complete: four stages - egg, larva, pupa, adult; larva very different from adult
1 mark: (b) Example of complete: butterfly/housefly/mosquito/beetle
2 marks: (b) Incomplete: three stages - egg, nymph, adult; nymph resembles adult but lacks wings/reproductive organs
1 mark: (b) Example of incomplete: cockroach/grasshopper/termite
2 marks: (c) Female lays eggs on leaves of the food plant; eggs hatch into larvae (caterpillars)
2 marks: (c) Caterpillar feeds voraciously on leaves, grows and moults several times
2 marks: (c) Mature larva becomes a pupa (chrysalis), attached to a support; it does not feed
2 marks: (c) Inside the pupa, tissues are reorganised; the adult (imago) emerges, dries and expands its wings
2 marks: (d) Any two, 1 mark each: caterpillars eat crop leaves and reduce yield; bore into fruits/stems; defoliate seedlings
2 marks: (d) Any one control measure: hand-picking larvae; spraying insecticide; biological control with parasitic wasps/birds
questions.explanation: Metamorphosis is the change of form during development. Complete metamorphosis (butterfly) has egg, larva, pupa and adult; incomplete (cockroach) has egg, nymph and adult. A butterfly lays eggs on leaves; caterpillars hatch, feed and moult; they pupate and the adult emerges. Caterpillars damage crops by eating leaves and can be controlled by hand-picking, insecticides or natural enemies.

questions.stem:
(a) Why is it necessary for fruits and seeds to be dispersed? Give three reasons. [3 marks]
(b) Name four agents of dispersal and, for each, name one fruit or seed dispersed by it and one feature of the fruit or seed that adapts it to that agent. [12 marks]
(c) Classify each of the following fruits as fleshy or dry: orange, groundnut, mango, cotton, tomato. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Any three, 1 mark each: avoid overcrowding/competition with parent; colonise new areas; reduce spread of disease and pests among offspring; ensure survival of the species
3 marks: (b) Wind: e.g. Tridax/cotton/Combretum; feature: hairs/pappus, wings, light weight (1 mark agent, 1 example, 1 feature)
3 marks: (b) Water: e.g. coconut; feature: fibrous, air-filled mesocarp, waterproof exocarp
3 marks: (b) Animals: e.g. Desmodium/Boerhavia (hooks) or mango/guava (edible, coloured); feature: hooks/sticky or succulent coloured pericarp
3 marks: (b) Self/explosive: e.g. Crotalaria/balsam/African yam bean pod; feature: pod dries and splits suddenly with force
5 marks: (c) 1 mark each: orange - fleshy; groundnut - dry; mango - fleshy; cotton - dry; tomato - fleshy
questions.explanation: Dispersal prevents overcrowding and competition, allows colonisation and survival. Wind disperses light, hairy or winged fruits like Tridax; water disperses coconut with its buoyant fibrous husk; animals carry hooked fruits like Desmodium or eat fleshy ones like guava; explosive pods like Crotalaria fling seeds out. Orange, mango and tomato are fleshy; groundnut and cotton are dry.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between macronutrients and micronutrients in plants, giving two examples of each. [6 marks]
(b) For each of the following elements, state one function in the plant and one deficiency symptom: (i) nitrogen; (ii) phosphorus; (iii) magnesium; (iv) potassium. [8 marks]
(c) Describe how water culture experiments can be used to show that a plant needs a particular mineral element. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Macronutrients: required in large quantities
2 marks: (a) Two examples, e.g. N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S (1 mark each)
1 mark: (a) Micronutrients: required in very small (trace) quantities
2 marks: (a) Two examples, e.g. Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) N: forms proteins/chlorophyll; deficiency - stunted growth, yellow leaves (chlorosis)
2 marks: (b)(ii) P: forms ATP/nucleic acids, root development; deficiency - poor root growth, purplish leaves, stunting
2 marks: (b)(iii) Mg: part of chlorophyll; deficiency - chlorosis between veins of older leaves
2 marks: (b)(iv) K: enzyme activation/stomatal movement; deficiency - scorched/yellow leaf margins, weak stems
2 marks: (c) Prepare a complete culture solution and others each lacking one element; grow similar seedlings in each
2 marks: (c) Wrap culture vessels in black paper (prevent algae), aerate the solutions, keep under the same conditions
2 marks: (c) After some weeks compare growth: seedlings lacking an element show poor growth/deficiency symptoms compared with the control in the complete solution
questions.explanation: Macronutrients (N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S) are needed in large amounts, micronutrients (Fe, Zn, B, Cu, Mn, Mo) in traces. Nitrogen builds proteins (lack: yellow, stunted plants); phosphorus builds ATP and roots (lack: purple leaves, poor roots); magnesium is in chlorophyll (lack: interveinal chlorosis); potassium activates enzymes (lack: scorched leaf edges). Water cultures with one element missing, compared with a complete solution, reveal its necessity.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a balanced diet? [2 marks]
(b) Name the class of food supplied mainly by each of the following: (i) yam; (ii) beans; (iii) palm oil; (iv) oranges; (v) fresh vegetables (as roughage). [5 marks]
(c) Name one deficiency disease caused by lack of each of the following and state one symptom of each: (i) vitamin C; (ii) vitamin D; (iii) iodine; (iv) iron. [8 marks]
(d) Explain why the following people need special diets: (i) a growing child; (ii) a pregnant woman; (iii) a labourer. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A diet containing all the classes of food (carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins, mineral salts, water, roughage) in the right proportions for the needs of the individual
5 marks: (b) 1 mark each: (i) carbohydrate; (ii) protein; (iii) fat/oil; (iv) vitamin (C); (v) roughage/fibre
2 marks: (c)(i) Scurvy; bleeding gums/slow wound healing
2 marks: (c)(ii) Rickets; soft, bent (bow) legs
2 marks: (c)(iii) Goitre; swelling of the neck (thyroid)
2 marks: (c)(iv) Anaemia; tiredness/pale skin/shortness of breath
2 marks: (d)(i) Child needs more protein for growth and calcium for bones
2 marks: (d)(ii) Pregnant woman needs more protein, iron, calcium and vitamins for the developing foetus
1 mark: (d)(iii) Labourer needs more energy foods (carbohydrates/fats) for heavy work
questions.explanation: A balanced diet contains all food classes in correct proportions. Yam gives carbohydrate, beans protein, palm oil fat, oranges vitamin C and vegetables roughage. Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, vitamin D rickets, iodine goitre and iron anaemia. Children need protein and calcium, pregnant women protein, iron and calcium, labourers more energy foods.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the four chambers of the stomach of a cow in the order in which food first passes through them. [4 marks]
(b) Describe how a cow digests the cellulose in grass. [8 marks]
(c) Give four differences between the alimentary canal of a ruminant and that of a carnivore such as a dog. [4 marks]
(d) State four features of the teeth of a dog that adapt it to its diet. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) 1 mark each in order: rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum
2 marks: (b) Grass is chewed briefly, mixed with saliva and swallowed into the rumen
2 marks: (b) In the rumen, bacteria and protozoa produce cellulase which breaks down cellulose (fermentation) into fatty acids absorbed by the cow
2 marks: (b) Food passes to the reticulum, forms the cud which is regurgitated and chewed again (rumination), then swallowed
2 marks: (b) It passes to the omasum (water absorbed) and to the abomasum (true stomach) where enzymes digest the food and microbes; digestion is completed in the intestine
4 marks: (c) Any four contrasts, 1 mark each: ruminant has four-chambered stomach, dog one; ruminant intestine very long, dog short; ruminant has large caecum, dog small; ruminant harbours cellulose-digesting microbes, dog does not; ruminant regurgitates/chews cud, dog does not
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: sharp incisors for gripping/cutting; long pointed canines for seizing and tearing; carnassial teeth for shearing flesh; sharp-pointed premolars and molars for cutting/crushing bones; no diastema
questions.explanation: Food passes through the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Microbes in the rumen ferment cellulose; cud is regurgitated and re-chewed, water is absorbed in the omasum and enzymes act in the abomasum. Ruminants have a four-chambered stomach, long gut and large caecum; a dog has a simple stomach and short gut. Dog teeth include long canines and shearing carnassials for a flesh diet.

questions.stem:
(a) What is ecological succession? [2 marks]
(b) Distinguish between primary and secondary succession, giving one example of where each may occur. [6 marks]
(c) Describe the stages of succession on a bare rock surface until a forest is formed. [8 marks]
(d) State four characteristics of a climax community. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The gradual and orderly replacement of one community of organisms by another in an area over time until a stable (climax) community is reached
2 marks: (b) Primary: begins on a bare area where no soil or life existed before
1 mark: (b) Example: bare rock, new volcanic lava, sand dune
2 marks: (b) Secondary: begins in an area where a community existed but was disturbed/removed, and soil remains
1 mark: (b) Example: abandoned farmland, burnt bush, cleared forest
2 marks: (c) Pioneer lichens colonise the bare rock, secrete acids and start to break it down; dead lichens add humus
2 marks: (c) Mosses grow in the thin soil and add more organic matter
2 marks: (c) Ferns and grasses/herbs follow as the soil deepens, then shrubs replace them
2 marks: (c) Trees establish, shade out the shrubs and a forest (climax) is formed
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: stable over a long period; high species diversity; complex food webs; dominated by large plants (trees); in balance with climate; little change in biomass
questions.explanation: Succession is the orderly change of communities to a climax. Primary succession starts on bare ground without soil (rock, lava); secondary starts where soil remains (abandoned farmland). On bare rock lichens come first, then mosses, ferns and grasses, shrubs and finally trees. Climax communities are stable, diverse and in equilibrium with the climate.

questions.stem:
(a) Name four sources of water pollution in Nigeria. [4 marks]
(b) Explain how an oil spill in a creek of the Niger Delta affects (i) fish; (ii) mangrove plants; (iii) the people living nearby. [9 marks]
(c) State three effects of excessive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides on soil. [3 marks]
(d) Suggest four ways of reducing water and soil pollution. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any four, 1 mark each: crude oil spills; industrial effluent; sewage/human excreta; refuse dumping; fertiliser/pesticide run-off; mining wastes; illegal refining
3 marks: (b)(i) Oil forms a film on the surface reducing oxygen dissolving into water; oil clogs gills; toxic components kill fish/eggs; fish become tainted
3 marks: (b)(ii) Oil coats roots/pneumatophores and leaves, preventing gaseous exchange and photosynthesis; mangroves die
3 marks: (b)(iii) Loss of fishing livelihood; contaminated drinking water causes illness; loss of farmland; food shortage/poverty
3 marks: (c) Any three, 1 mark each: kill useful soil organisms; change soil pH (acidity); accumulate toxic residues; destroy soil structure; contaminate groundwater
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: treat sewage and industrial effluent before discharge; prompt clean-up of oil spills/maintain pipelines; proper refuse disposal; use organic manure and integrated pest management; enforce environmental laws; public enlightenment
questions.explanation: Oil spills, industrial and domestic effluents, refuse and agrochemical run-off pollute water. Oil films cut off oxygen and suffocate fish, coat mangrove roots so they cannot breathe, and destroy the livelihood and health of local people. Over-use of chemicals kills soil organisms, acidifies soil and leaves residues. Treatment of effluents, spill clean-up, proper waste disposal, organic farming and enforcement of laws reduce pollution.

questions.topic: Linkage, sex determination and sex-linked characters
questions.stem:
(a) Explain, using a genetic diagram, why the number of boys and girls born in a large population is approximately equal. [6 marks]
(b) What is a sex-linked character? Give two examples in humans. [3 marks]
(c) Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele (h) carried on the X chromosome. A woman who is a carrier marries a man with normal blood clotting. (i) Write the genotypes of the parents. (ii) Using a genetic diagram, work out the possible genotypes of their children. (iii) What proportion of their sons are expected to be haemophiliac? (iv) What proportion of their daughters are expected to be carriers? [11 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Parents: female XX x male XY
2 marks: (a) Gametes: female produces only X eggs; male produces X and Y sperms in equal numbers
2 marks: (a) Offspring: XX : XY in ratio 1 : 1, i.e. 50% girls and 50% boys
1 mark: (b) A character controlled by a gene carried on a sex chromosome (usually the X)
2 marks: (b) Any two, 1 mark each: haemophilia; red-green colour blindness; Duchenne muscular dystrophy; baldness (sex-influenced accepted)
2 marks: (c)(i) Woman XHXh; man XHY (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c)(ii) Gametes: XH, Xh from mother; XH, Y from father
3 marks: (c)(ii) Offspring: XHXH (normal girl), XHXh (carrier girl), XHY (normal boy), XhY (haemophiliac boy)
2 marks: (c)(iii) 1/2 (50%) of sons
2 marks: (c)(iv) 1/2 (50%) of daughters
questions.explanation: XX x XY gives X eggs and equal numbers of X and Y sperms, so offspring are 1 XX : 1 XY. Sex-linked genes lie on the X chromosome, e.g. haemophilia and colour blindness. XHXh x XHY gives XHXH, XHXh, XHY and XhY: half the sons are haemophiliac and half the daughters are carriers.

questions.stem:
(a) What is organic evolution? [2 marks]
(b) Explain how each of the following provides evidence for evolution: (i) fossil records; (ii) comparative anatomy; (iii) comparative embryology; (iv) geographical distribution. [12 marks]
(c) Distinguish between homologous and analogous structures, giving one example of each. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The gradual change in the characteristics of organisms over many generations, giving rise to new species from pre-existing ones
3 marks: (b)(i) Fossils in older (lower) rock layers are simpler; younger layers contain more complex forms; series of fossils (e.g. horse) show gradual change
3 marks: (b)(ii) Similar basic structures (e.g. pentadactyl limb) in different organisms suggest common ancestry; vestigial organs such as the appendix
3 marks: (b)(iii) Early embryos of different vertebrates are very similar (gill slits, tail), indicating common ancestry
3 marks: (b)(iv) Isolated areas have distinct species (e.g. Australia marsupials, Galapagos finches), suggesting evolution after separation from a common ancestor
1 mark: (c) Homologous: same basic structure and origin but different functions
2 marks: (c) Example: forelimb of man, wing of bat, flipper of whale
1 mark: (c) Analogous: different structure and origin but same function
2 marks: (c) Example: wing of a bird and wing of an insect
questions.explanation: Evolution is gradual change producing new species. Fossils show increasing complexity in younger rocks; comparative anatomy shows shared structures like the pentadactyl limb; embryos of vertebrates are alike early on; isolated regions have unique species. Homologous structures share origin but differ in function (bat wing, human arm); analogous ones share function but not origin (bird and insect wings).

questions.stem:
(a) What is variation? [2 marks]
(b) Distinguish between continuous and discontinuous variation, giving two examples of each in humans. [8 marks]
(c) State four causes of variation among organisms. [4 marks]
(d) Explain three ways in which knowledge of variation is applied in (i) crime detection; (ii) agriculture. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The differences that exist among individuals of the same species
2 marks: (b) Continuous: shows a gradual range of values between extremes, with intermediates; usually affected by environment and many genes
2 marks: (b) Examples: height, weight, skin colour, intelligence (any two)
2 marks: (b) Discontinuous: clear-cut categories with no intermediates; usually controlled by one or few genes
2 marks: (b) Examples: blood group, tongue rolling, sex, ability to taste PTC, albinism (any two)
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: crossing over in meiosis; random assortment of chromosomes; random fertilisation; mutation; environmental factors (diet, climate)
3 marks: (d)(i) Fingerprints are unique to each person; blood group tests; DNA fingerprinting identifies suspects/victims (any three, 1 mark each)
3 marks: (d)(ii) Selection of high-yielding, disease-resistant varieties; breeding animals for desirable traits; hybridisation for hybrid vigour (any three, 1 mark each)
questions.explanation: Variation is the difference among individuals of a species. Continuous variation (height, weight) shows a range; discontinuous (blood group, tongue rolling) falls into distinct classes. Causes include crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation, mutation and environment. Fingerprints, blood groups and DNA profiles aid crime detection; selection and breeding of superior plants and animals apply variation in agriculture.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a social animal? [2 marks]
(b) Name the castes found in a termite colony and state two functions of each caste. [10 marks]
(c) State four advantages of social life to termites. [4 marks]
(d) State two harmful and two beneficial effects of termites to man. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) An animal that lives in an organised group (colony) of the same species in which members co-operate and share duties (division of labour)
3 marks: (b) Workers: build and repair the nest; collect food and feed others; care for eggs and young; groom the queen (any two) + naming
3 marks: (b) Soldiers: defend the colony with large mandibles or chemical spray; guard the entrances (two functions) + naming
2 marks: (b) Queen: lays eggs; produces substances (pheromones) that control the colony
2 marks: (b) King: fertilises the queen; stays with her in the royal chamber / alates (winged reproductives): start new colonies
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: division of labour increases efficiency; better defence; shared food; care of young; better nest building/microclimate control; rapid reproduction
2 marks: (d) Harmful, any two: destroy wooden buildings/furniture; damage crops; destroy books/clothes
2 marks: (d) Beneficial, any two: improve soil aeration/mixing; decompose dead matter; alates eaten as food; anthill soil used for building
questions.explanation: A social animal lives in an organised colony with division of labour. Termites have workers (build, feed, nurse), soldiers (defend), a queen (lays eggs) and a king (mates); winged alates found new colonies. Social life gives efficiency, protection, food sharing and care of young. Termites damage wood and crops but aerate soil, recycle dead matter and are eaten as food.

questions.stem:
Study the specimens described below, all collected around a school farm in Ogbomoso, and answer the questions.
Specimen E: a long, soft, cylindrical animal with a body divided into many similar rings; it has no legs, a thickened band (clitellum) near the front end and tiny bristles on the underside; its skin is moist.
Specimen F: an animal with a soft unsegmented body partly enclosed in a coiled, hard shell; it has a muscular flat foot and two pairs of tentacles on the head, the longer pair bearing eyes at their tips.
Specimen G: a long, cylindrical, segmented animal with a hard covering; it has two pairs of jointed legs on most body segments and curls into a coil when touched.
Specimen H: an animal with a hard covering, four pairs of jointed walking legs, a pair of large pincers in front and a narrow segmented tail ending in a curved sting.
(a) Name the phylum to which each of specimens E, F, G and H belongs. [4 marks]
(b) Give the common name of each of specimens E, F, G and H. [4 marks]
(c) Name the class of (i) specimen G; (ii) specimen H. [2 marks]
(d) State three features, from the descriptions, that specimens G and H share which place them in the same phylum. [3 marks]
(e) State two differences between specimen E and specimen G that can be observed. [4 marks]
(f) (i) State the function of the bristles on specimen E. (ii) Explain why specimen E must keep its skin moist. [4 marks]
(g) State two ways in which specimen F is adapted for life on land and two ways in which specimen E is useful to the farmer. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) E - Annelida; F - Mollusca; G - Arthropoda; H - Arthropoda (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b) E - earthworm; F - land snail (giant African snail); G - millipede; H - scorpion (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) (i) G - Diplopoda (Myriapoda accepted); (ii) H - Arachnida (1 mark each)
3 marks: (d) Hard exoskeleton; jointed legs/appendages; segmented body (1 mark each)
4 marks: (e) Any two, 2 marks each: E soft moist body, G hard exoskeleton; E has no legs, G has jointed legs; E has clitellum, G has none; E has chaetae/bristles, G has none
2 marks: (f)(i) Chaetae grip the soil/burrow walls during movement (locomotion)
2 marks: (f)(ii) Gaseous exchange takes place through the skin; oxygen must dissolve in the moisture before diffusing in
2 marks: (g) F: shell prevents drying out/protects; secretes mucus/slime to move and reduce water loss; withdraws into shell in dry weather (any two, 1 mark each)
2 marks: (g) E: burrowing aerates and drains the soil; mixes soil layers; worm casts add humus/fertility (any two, 1 mark each)
questions.explanation: E is an earthworm (Annelida), F a land snail (Mollusca), G a millipede (Arthropoda, Diplopoda) and H a scorpion (Arthropoda, Arachnida). Arthropods share an exoskeleton, jointed legs and segmentation. The earthworm uses chaetae for grip and breathes through its moist skin; it aerates and enriches soil. The snail resists drying with its shell and mucus.

questions.stem:
A student tied one end of a length of visking (dialysis) tubing, filled it with 20% sucrose solution and fitted the open end tightly to a narrow glass capillary tube. The tubing was lowered into a beaker of distilled water and the level of liquid in the capillary tube was marked at time zero. The rise in level was recorded every 5 minutes:
Time (min): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25
Rise in level (mm): 0, 6, 12, 17, 21, 24
(a) Name the process responsible for the rise in level. [1 mark]
(b) Explain why the level in the capillary tube rose. [4 marks]
(c) Calculate the average rate of rise in mm per minute (i) during the first 10 minutes; (ii) between the 15th and 25th minutes; (iii) over the whole 25 minutes. Show your working. [6 marks]
(d) Suggest a reason for the difference between your answers to (c)(i) and (c)(ii). [2 marks]
(e) State what would happen to the level if the beaker contained 40% sucrose solution instead of distilled water. Give a reason. [3 marks]
(f) Describe a suitable control for this experiment. [2 marks]
(g) State three precautions that should be taken in this experiment. [3 marks]
(h) State two ways in which the process in (a) is important to living plants. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Osmosis
2 marks: (b) Visking tubing is partially (selectively) permeable; water molecules pass through but sucrose molecules are too large
2 marks: (b) Water moves from the distilled water (higher water potential) into the sucrose solution (lower water potential), increasing the volume inside and pushing the liquid up the capillary
2 marks: (c)(i) 12 mm / 10 min = 1.2 mm per minute
2 marks: (c)(ii) (24 - 17) mm / 10 min = 7 / 10 = 0.7 mm per minute
2 marks: (c)(iii) 24 mm / 25 min = 0.96 mm per minute
2 marks: (d) As water enters, the sucrose solution becomes more dilute and the concentration gradient falls; the column of liquid also exerts back pressure, so the rate slows
1 mark: (e) The level would fall
2 marks: (e) The outside solution is more concentrated, so water moves out of the tubing by osmosis
2 marks: (f) Identical set-up with distilled water (instead of sucrose) in the tubing; the level does not rise
3 marks: (g) Any three, 1 mark each: tie the tubing tightly to avoid leakage; rinse the outside of the tubing to remove sucrose; read the level at eye level; keep temperature constant; start timing immediately; make sure the tubing has no holes
4 marks: (h) Any two, 2 marks each: absorption of water by root hairs; movement of water from cell to cell; keeps cells turgid for support; opening and closing of stomata (guard cells)
questions.explanation: Water enters the tubing by osmosis because the membrane lets water but not sucrose through. Rates: 12/10 = 1.2 mm/min, 7/10 = 0.7 mm/min and 24/25 = 0.96 mm/min; the rate falls as the solution is diluted and hydrostatic pressure rises. With 40% sucrose outside, water leaves and the level falls. A control has distilled water inside the tubing.

questions.stem:
Two vacuum flasks, A and B, were each three-quarters filled with soaked bean seeds. The seeds in A were germinating. The seeds in B had been boiled and then washed in dilute formalin (disinfectant). A thermometer was fixed through a cotton-wool plug in the mouth of each flask, and both flasks were inverted. The temperature in each flask was read at the same time each day:
Day: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Flask A (oC): 28.0, 31.0, 34.0, 36.0, 37.0
Flask B (oC): 28.0, 28.0, 28.5, 28.0, 28.0
(a) State the aim of this experiment. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate (i) the total rise in temperature in flask A over the four days; (ii) the mean daily rise in temperature in flask A. [4 marks]
(c) Explain the change in temperature in flask A. [3 marks]
(d) Give reasons for each of the following: (i) the seeds in B were boiled; (ii) the seeds in B were washed in formalin; (iii) a vacuum flask was used; (iv) the flasks were inverted. [8 marks]
(e) Write a word equation for aerobic respiration in the seeds. [2 marks]
(f) Suggest why the rise in temperature in A became smaller after day 3. [2 marks]
(g) Name the substance that could be used to show that the germinating seeds release carbon dioxide and state the result expected. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) To show that germinating (living) seeds release heat (energy) during respiration
2 marks: (b)(i) 37.0 - 28.0 = 9.0 oC
2 marks: (b)(ii) 9.0 / 4 = 2.25 oC per day
3 marks: (c) Germinating seeds respire actively; respiration releases energy, some of it as heat; the vacuum flask prevents heat loss, so temperature rises
2 marks: (d)(i) Boiling kills the seeds so they cannot respire (serves as control)
2 marks: (d)(ii) Formalin kills micro-organisms on the seeds, which would otherwise respire/decompose them and produce heat
2 marks: (d)(iii) Vacuum flask insulates, preventing loss of heat to the surroundings
2 marks: (d)(iv) Carbon dioxide is denser than air and sinks to the mouth, escaping through the cotton wool so it does not suffocate the seeds / heat rising is trapped around the seeds
2 marks: (e) Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
2 marks: (f) Oxygen in the flask becomes depleted / food reserves fall / accumulation of carbon dioxide slows respiration
2 marks: (g) Lime water / sodium hydrogencarbonate indicator
2 marks: (g) Lime water turns milky (indicator turns from red to yellow)
questions.explanation: Flask A rose by 37.0 - 28.0 = 9.0 oC, i.e. 2.25 oC per day, because germinating seeds respire and release heat that the vacuum flask retains. Boiled, disinfected seeds in B are a control with no living tissue or microbes. Inversion lets CO2 escape through the cotton wool. Respiration slows as oxygen runs low. Lime water turning milky shows CO2.

questions.stem:
A shoot of the pondweed Elodea was placed upside down in a test tube of pond water to which a little sodium hydrogencarbonate had been added. A bench lamp was placed at different distances from the tube and, after allowing 3 minutes at each distance, the number of gas bubbles released from the cut end in 5 minutes was counted. The temperature was kept at 27 oC.
Distance of lamp (cm): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Bubbles in 5 minutes: 150, 80, 38, 22, 15
(a) Calculate the rate of bubbling (bubbles per minute) at each distance. [5 marks]
(b) Light intensity is proportional to 1/d2, where d is the distance of the lamp. Calculate the relative light intensity, 1000/d2, at each distance. [5 marks]
(c) Describe the relationship between light intensity and the rate of bubbling. [2 marks]
(d) Name the gas in the bubbles and describe a test to confirm it. [3 marks]
(e) Give reasons for (i) adding sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water; (ii) waiting 3 minutes at each new distance; (iii) keeping the temperature constant. [6 marks]
(f) State two sources of error in counting bubbles as a measure of photosynthesis. [2 marks]
(g) Name one factor, other than light, that could limit the rate at the 10 cm distance. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) 150/5 = 30; 80/5 = 16; 38/5 = 7.6; 22/5 = 4.4; 15/5 = 3.0 bubbles per minute (1 mark each)
5 marks: (b) 1000/100 = 10.0; 1000/400 = 2.5; 1000/900 = 1.11; 1000/1600 = 0.625 (0.63); 1000/2500 = 0.40 (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) The rate of bubbling (photosynthesis) increases as light intensity increases
1 mark: (d) Oxygen
2 marks: (d) Collect the gas in an inverted tube; a glowing splint relights
2 marks: (e)(i) It supplies carbon dioxide (raw material) so that CO2 does not limit the rate
2 marks: (e)(ii) To allow the plant to adjust to the new light intensity before counting
2 marks: (e)(iii) Temperature affects enzyme activity/rate of photosynthesis; it must not vary so that only light is tested; the lamp also heats the water
2 marks: (f) Any two, 1 mark each: bubbles differ in size; some oxygen dissolves in the water; gas may contain nitrogen/CO2; counting mistakes; some oxygen used in respiration
2 marks: (g) Carbon dioxide concentration / temperature / amount of chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Rates are 30, 16, 7.6, 4.4 and 3.0 bubbles per minute; relative intensities 1000/d2 are 10.0, 2.5, 1.11, 0.625 and 0.40. Bubbling rises with light intensity. The gas is oxygen (relights a glowing splint). Hydrogencarbonate supplies CO2; acclimatisation and constant temperature ensure a fair test. Bubble size varies and some oxygen dissolves. At close range CO2 or temperature may limit the rate.

questions.stem:
Four leafy shoots of Hibiscus of about the same size, P, Q, R and S, were each placed in a test tube of water covered with a thin layer of oil. Before the experiment, petroleum jelly (Vaseline) was applied as follows: P - no jelly; Q - upper surfaces of all leaves; R - lower surfaces of all leaves; S - both surfaces of all leaves. Each tube with its shoot weighed 20.0 g at the start. After 24 hours in a well-lit, airy room, the masses were: P - 15.2 g; Q - 16.0 g; R - 19.0 g; S - 19.8 g.
(a) Calculate the loss in mass of each set-up. [4 marks]
(b) Calculate the loss in mass of each set-up as a percentage of its starting mass. [4 marks]
(c) Explain why a layer of oil was placed on the water. [2 marks]
(d) What does the result for (i) set-up Q; (ii) set-up R suggest about the distribution of stomata on Hibiscus leaves? [4 marks]
(e) Account for the small loss in mass by set-up S. [2 marks]
(f) Explain why the room was well-lit and airy. [3 marks]
(g) Describe a quick test, using cobalt chloride paper, to confirm your conclusion in (d). [4 marks]
(h) State two ways in which transpiration is useful to the plant. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) P: 20.0 - 15.2 = 4.8 g; Q: 4.0 g; R: 1.0 g; S: 0.2 g (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b) P: 4.8/20 x 100 = 24%; Q: 20%; R: 5%; S: 1% (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) To prevent evaporation of water directly from the water surface, so that all loss is through the shoot
2 marks: (d)(i) Q lost much water with the upper surface blocked, so most water escapes through the lower surface: the lower surface has more stomata
2 marks: (d)(ii) R lost little water with the lower surface blocked, so the upper surface has few stomata
2 marks: (e) Water was lost through the stem (lenticels/cuticle) and slight leakage through imperfectly covered areas
3 marks: (f) Light opens stomata; moving air removes water vapour from around the leaves, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient; this gives a measurable rate
2 marks: (g) Place dry blue cobalt chloride paper on both surfaces of a leaf, cover with glass slides and clip
2 marks: (g) The paper on the lower surface turns pink faster than that on the upper surface
2 marks: (h) Any two, 1 mark each: cools the leaves; helps upward movement of water and mineral salts; keeps cells turgid; supplies water for photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Losses are 4.8, 4.0, 1.0 and 0.2 g, i.e. 24%, 20%, 5% and 1%. Blocking the lower surface (R) stopped most water loss, showing that most stomata are on the lower surface. The oil prevents direct evaporation; S still loses a little through the stem and cuticle. Cobalt chloride paper turns pink faster on the lower surface. Transpiration cools leaves and draws water and minerals upward.

questions.stem:
Study the two flowers described below and answer the questions.
Specimen K (Allamanda): a large, bright yellow, funnel-shaped flower; five green sepals are free; the five petals are joined to form a tube that opens into five broad lobes; five stamens are attached to the inside of the corolla tube; the ovary is superior and is surrounded by a ring-shaped disc; nectar is present at the base of the tube.
Specimen L (Crotalaria): a yellow flower borne on an upright spike; five sepals are joined; the corolla has one large upright standard petal, two side wing petals and two lower petals joined to form a boat-shaped keel that encloses ten stamens and a long curved style; the ovary is a single carpel.
(a) State the symmetry of (i) specimen K; (ii) specimen L. [2 marks]
(b) Describe the corolla of (i) specimen K; (ii) specimen L, using correct terms. [4 marks]
(c) State whether each flower is hypogynous, perigynous or epigynous. [2 marks]
(d) Name the family to which specimen L belongs and name one food crop in the same family. [2 marks]
(e) Write the floral formula of specimen K, using K for calyx, C for corolla, A for androecium and G for gynoecium (assume two fused carpels). [4 marks]
(f) State three features of specimen K that suggest it is insect-pollinated. [3 marks]
(g) Explain how the keel of specimen L ensures pollination by a visiting bee. [4 marks]
(h) Name the fruit type formed by specimen L and state how its seeds are dispersed. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) (i) K - actinomorphic (radial symmetry); (ii) L - zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) K: gamopetalous (petals fused), funnel-shaped/infundibuliform, five-lobed
2 marks: (b)(ii) L: polypetalous/papilionaceous corolla with standard, two wings and keel
2 marks: (c) Both hypogynous (superior ovary) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (d) Papilionaceae / Fabaceae (Leguminosae) (1 mark); cowpea / groundnut / soya bean (1 mark)
4 marks: (e) Actinomorphic symbol (or Act.) K5 C(5) A5 G(2) - correct symmetry sign, K5, C(5) with stamens epipetalous, G(2) superior (1 mark each part)
3 marks: (f) Any three, 1 mark each: large flower; bright yellow colour; nectar present; stamens enclosed in tube; scent
2 marks: (g) The bee lands on the wing and keel petals; its weight pushes the keel down
2 marks: (g) The stamens and stigma spring out and touch the underside of the bee, depositing pollen and picking up pollen from previous flowers
2 marks: (h) Legume (pod)
2 marks: (h) The pod dries and splits explosively along two sutures, throwing out the seeds (self/explosive dispersal)
questions.explanation: K is radially symmetrical with a gamopetalous funnel-shaped corolla; L is zygomorphic with a papilionaceous corolla (standard, wings, keel). Both are hypogynous. L belongs to Fabaceae (Papilionaceae), like cowpea. K: Act. K5 C(5) A5 G(2). K is large, bright and nectariferous, attracting insects. A bee pressing on the keel exposes stamens and stigma. L forms a legume that splits explosively.

questions.stem:
Study the fruits and seeds described below and answer the questions.
Specimen M: a dry, ovoid fruit about 25 cm long with a smooth green-brown outer skin, a thick layer of loose fibres beneath it and a very hard, stony inner layer with three "eyes" at one end.
Specimen N: a small, dry, one-seeded fruit about 3 mm long crowned with a ring of fine, feathery hairs; collected from a weed (Tridax) growing on the school field.
Specimen O: a dry, flattened pod about 20 cm long which, when ripe, twists sharply along its two edges and throws out the seeds.
Specimen Q: a ripe guava fruit with a yellow skin, a soft sweet pink flesh and many small hard seeds.
Specimen R: a small, flat, dry fruit covered with tiny hooked hairs, collected from the socks of a student after walking through a bush path.
(a) State the agent of dispersal of each of specimens M, N, O, Q and R. [5 marks]
(b) For each specimen, state one feature, from the description, that adapts it to the agent stated in (a). [5 marks]
(c) Name the part of specimen M that (i) helps it to float; (ii) protects the seed. [2 marks]
(d) Classify specimens M, O and Q as fleshy or dry, dehiscent or indehiscent. [6 marks]
(e) Explain why the seeds of specimen Q are able to pass through the gut of a bird unharmed. [2 marks]
(f) Name the type of fruit represented by specimen O. [1 mark]
(g) State two advantages to a plant of having its seeds dispersed far away from the parent and two disadvantages of dispersal by animals. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) M - water; N - wind; O - self (explosive mechanism); Q - animals (eaten); R - animals (attached to fur/clothing) (1 mark each)
5 marks: (b) M - fibrous, air-filled mesocarp/light; N - pappus of feathery hairs (parachute); O - pod dries and splits/twists with force; Q - brightly coloured, sweet edible flesh; R - hooked hairs (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) (i) Fibrous mesocarp; (ii) hard stony endocarp (1 mark each)
6 marks: (d) M - dry, indehiscent; O - dry, dehiscent; Q - fleshy, indehiscent (1 mark each property)
2 marks: (e) The seeds have hard, resistant seed coats that are not digested by enzymes
1 mark: (f) Legume / pod
2 marks: (g) Advantages, any two: avoids overcrowding/competition; colonisation of new areas; reduces spread of disease from parent
2 marks: (g) Disadvantages, any two: seeds may be dropped in unsuitable places; many seeds are digested/destroyed; seeds may be carried too far
questions.explanation: Coconut (M) floats on water due to its fibrous mesocarp, Tridax (N) is wind-dispersed by its pappus, the pod O disperses explosively, guava (Q) is eaten by animals, and the hooked fruit R clings to clothing and fur. M is dry indehiscent, O dry dehiscent and Q fleshy indehiscent. Hard seed coats survive digestion. Dispersal reduces competition but animals may drop seeds in poor places.

questions.stem:
A pure-breeding tall bean plant was crossed with a pure-breeding dwarf bean plant. All the F1 plants were tall. The F1 plants were allowed to self-pollinate and 810 F2 plants were raised. Of these, 612 were tall and 198 were dwarf.
(a) Using T for the allele for tallness and t for dwarfness, write the genotypes of (i) the tall parent; (ii) the dwarf parent; (iii) the F1 plants. [3 marks]
(b) Which character is dominant? Give a reason for your answer. [2 marks]
(c) Draw a genetic diagram (Punnett square) to show the cross between two F1 plants. [5 marks]
(d) (i) Calculate the observed ratio of tall to dwarf plants in the F2, to two decimal places. (ii) Calculate the expected numbers of tall and dwarf plants out of 810 according to Mendel's ratio. [6 marks]
(e) Give one reason why the observed numbers differ slightly from the expected numbers. [2 marks]
(f) What fraction of the tall F2 plants would be expected to be heterozygous? [2 marks]
(g) Describe how a farmer could find out whether a particular tall F2 plant is homozygous or heterozygous. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) (i) TT; (ii) tt; (iii) Tt (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) Tall (1 mark); it appears in all the F1 plants although both alleles are present / it masks dwarfness (1 mark)
2 marks: (c) Parents Tt x Tt; gametes T, t from each parent
2 marks: (c) Offspring TT, Tt, Tt, tt correctly shown in Punnett square
1 mark: (c) Phenotypes: 3 tall : 1 dwarf
3 marks: (d)(i) 612 / 198 = 3.09, i.e. 3.09 : 1
3 marks: (d)(ii) Tall = 3/4 x 810 = 607.5 (about 608); dwarf = 1/4 x 810 = 202.5 (about 202/203)
2 marks: (e) Fertilisation is random / chance in the combination of gametes; some seeds may not germinate or plants may die
2 marks: (f) 2/3 (two out of every three tall plants are Tt)
2 marks: (g) Carry out a test cross: cross the tall plant with a dwarf (tt) plant
3 marks: (g) If all offspring are tall the plant is homozygous (TT); if about half are tall and half dwarf (1 : 1) the plant is heterozygous (Tt)
questions.explanation: Parents TT and tt give Tt F1 plants (tall is dominant). Tt x Tt gives TT, 2Tt, tt: 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Observed 612/198 = 3.09 : 1; expected 607.5 tall and 202.5 dwarf out of 810. Chance in fertilisation explains small differences. Two-thirds of tall F2 plants are Tt. A test cross with tt distinguishes TT (all tall) from Tt (1 tall : 1 dwarf).

questions.stem:
A small amount of yeast was added to 100 cm3 of sterile glucose solution in a flask kept at 30 oC. Each day a sample was taken and the number of yeast cells was counted with a haemocytometer. The results (thousands of cells per mm3) were:
Day: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
Number: 2, 4, 10, 28, 60, 85, 92, 93
(a) Describe the pattern of growth of the yeast population over the 7 days. [3 marks]
(b) Name the growth phases shown (i) between day 0 and day 1; (ii) between day 2 and day 5; (iii) between day 6 and day 7. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate (i) the increase in population between day 3 and day 4; (ii) the mean daily increase over the whole 7 days. [4 marks]
(d) Suggest two reasons why the population stopped increasing after day 6. [4 marks]
(e) Predict what would happen to the population if the experiment continued for another two weeks, and explain. [3 marks]
(f) State why (i) the glucose solution was sterile; (ii) the flask was kept at a constant temperature. [4 marks]
(g) Name two factors that increase and two factors that decrease the size of a natural animal population. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Slow increase at first; then rapid (exponential) increase from day 2 to day 5; then levelling off with little change from day 6 to day 7 (sigmoid curve)
3 marks: (b) (i) lag phase; (ii) log/exponential phase; (iii) stationary phase (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c)(i) 60 - 28 = 32 thousand cells per mm3
2 marks: (c)(ii) (93 - 2) / 7 = 91 / 7 = 13 thousand cells per mm3 per day
4 marks: (d) Any two, 2 marks each: glucose (food) being used up; accumulation of toxic wastes such as alcohol; shortage of space; decreasing oxygen; birth rate equals death rate
1 mark: (e) The population would decline (death phase)
2 marks: (e) Food is exhausted and alcohol concentration rises to toxic levels, so more cells die than are produced
2 marks: (f)(i) To prevent other micro-organisms competing with or contaminating the yeast
2 marks: (f)(ii) Temperature affects the rate of growth/reproduction; constant temperature ensures only time affects the result
2 marks: (g) Increase, any two: birth (natality); immigration; abundant food; absence of predators/disease
2 marks: (g) Decrease, any two: death (mortality); emigration; predation; disease; food shortage; competition
questions.explanation: The yeast shows a sigmoid curve: lag phase (days 0-1), exponential phase (days 2-5) and stationary phase (days 6-7). From day 3 to day 4 it rose by 60 - 28 = 32 thousand per mm3; the mean daily rise was 91/7 = 13 thousand. Growth stops as food runs out and alcohol accumulates; later a death phase follows. Sterility excludes competitors and constant temperature controls the rate.

questions.stem:
Study the insects described below and answer the questions.
Specimen S: a small brown beetle about 3 mm long with a long snout bearing jaws at its tip; found in stored maize grains with small round holes.
Specimen T: a large green insect with long hind legs, short antennae and two pairs of wings; found eating cassava leaves.
Specimen U: a tiny soft-bodied green insect clustered on the young shoots of cowpea; it has a needle-like mouthpart and two short tubes on its abdomen.
Specimen V: a red and black bug about 15 mm long found on open cotton bolls; the lint around its feeding sites is stained.
(a) Give the common name of each of specimens S, T, U and V. [4 marks]
(b) State the type of mouthpart of (i) specimens S and T; (ii) specimens U and V. [2 marks]
(c) Describe the type of damage caused by each specimen to the crop named. [8 marks]
(d) Explain why the insecticide used against specimen U should be a systemic one. [3 marks]
(e) Suggest one cultural and one chemical method of controlling specimen S in a store. [4 marks]
(f) State two advantages and two disadvantages of biological control of insect pests. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) S - maize weevil; T - grasshopper/variegated or green grasshopper (locust accepted); U - aphid; V - cotton stainer (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) (i) Biting and chewing; (ii) piercing and sucking (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) S: bores into grains, eats the endosperm, reduces weight and quality; holes allow moulds
2 marks: (c) T: eats leaves (defoliation), reducing photosynthesis and yield
2 marks: (c) U: sucks sap, causing curling/wilting and stunting; transmits viral diseases (e.g. cowpea mosaic)
2 marks: (c) V: sucks sap from developing seeds/bolls; stains lint and introduces fungi, lowering quality
3 marks: (d) Aphids suck sap from inside the plant; a systemic insecticide is absorbed and carried in the sap, so it kills the aphids as they feed; contact sprays may not reach those hidden on the undersides of leaves/shoots
2 marks: (e) Cultural: dry grains well before storage / clean and disinfest the store / store in airtight (hermetic) bags / early harvesting
2 marks: (e) Chemical: fumigation with phosphine (aluminium phosphide) tablets by a trained person / approved grain protectant dust
2 marks: (f) Advantages, any two: no chemical residue/pollution; cheap in the long run; self-sustaining; target-specific
2 marks: (f) Disadvantages, any two: slow to act; does not eradicate the pest; predator may attack useful organisms; requires expertise/research
questions.explanation: S is the maize weevil, T a grasshopper (biting and chewing), U an aphid and V a cotton stainer (piercing and sucking). Weevils hollow out grain, grasshoppers defoliate, aphids suck sap and spread viruses, and cotton stainers stain lint. Systemic insecticides move in the sap and reach sap-suckers. Drying grain and hermetic storage or professional fumigation control weevils. Biological control is safe and lasting but slow.

questions.stem:
The table below shows the concentration (g per 100 cm3) of some substances in the blood plasma entering a glomerulus, in the filtrate in Bowman's capsule and in the urine of a healthy man.
Substance: plasma / filtrate / urine
Protein: 8.00 / 0.00 / 0.00
Glucose: 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.00
Urea: 0.03 / 0.03 / 2.00
Mineral salts: 0.72 / 0.72 / 1.50
(a) Explain why protein is present in the plasma but absent from the filtrate. [3 marks]
(b) Explain why glucose is present in the filtrate but absent from the urine. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate how many times more concentrated (i) urea; (ii) mineral salts are in the urine than in the plasma. Give your answers to one decimal place. [4 marks]
(d) Explain why urea becomes so concentrated in the urine. [3 marks]
(e) The urine of a patient contains glucose. Name the likely disorder, the hormone involved and the organ that produces it. [3 marks]
(f) Name the part of the nephron where (i) ultrafiltration; (ii) most selective reabsorption take place. [2 marks]
(g) Describe a simple test to show the presence of glucose in a urine sample. [3 marks]
(h) State two ways of keeping the kidneys healthy. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Protein molecules are too large to pass through the walls of the glomerular capillaries and the basement membrane of Bowman's capsule, so they remain in the blood
3 marks: (b) Glucose is small and is filtered, but all of it is selectively (actively) reabsorbed into the blood in the proximal convoluted tubule
2 marks: (c)(i) Urea: 2.00 / 0.03 = 66.7 times
2 marks: (c)(ii) Salts: 1.50 / 0.72 = 2.1 times
3 marks: (d) Urea is not reabsorbed (little reabsorption), while most of the water is reabsorbed in the tubule and collecting duct, so the urea left becomes concentrated
1 mark: (e) Diabetes mellitus
1 mark: (e) Insulin
1 mark: (e) Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)
2 marks: (f) (i) Glomerulus/Bowman's capsule; (ii) proximal convoluted tubule (1 mark each)
1 mark: (g) Add Benedict's (or Fehling's) solution to a little urine
2 marks: (g) Heat in a boiling water bath; a green, yellow or brick-red precipitate shows glucose
4 marks: (h) Any two, 2 marks each: drink plenty of clean water; avoid misuse of drugs/painkillers; reduce salt intake; control blood pressure/blood sugar; avoid harmful herbal concoctions; treat infections promptly
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins are too large to be filtered. Glucose is filtered but fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Urea is concentrated 2.00/0.03 = 66.7 times and salts 1.50/0.72 = 2.1 times because water is reabsorbed while urea is not. Glucose in urine suggests diabetes mellitus from lack of insulin from the pancreas. Benedict's test detects glucose. Drinking water and avoiding drug misuse protect the kidneys.

questions.stem:
A student collected a sample of topsoil from a school garden in Owerri and carried out the following procedure.
1. Mass of empty evaporating dish = 25.0 g
2. Mass of dish + fresh soil = 75.0 g
3. The dish was heated in an oven at 105 oC, cooled and weighed repeatedly until the mass was constant: 67.5 g
4. The dried soil was then heated strongly over a Bunsen flame until it stopped glowing, cooled and weighed: 64.0 g
(a) Calculate the mass of fresh soil used. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate (i) the mass of water in the soil; (ii) the percentage of water in the fresh soil. [4 marks]
(c) Calculate (i) the mass of humus (organic matter) in the soil; (ii) the percentage of humus in the fresh soil; (iii) the percentage of humus in the dry soil, to one decimal place. [6 marks]
(d) Why was the soil heated to constant mass in step 3? [2 marks]
(e) Why was the temperature in step 3 kept at about 105 oC and not higher? [2 marks]
(f) Explain why the soil was cooled before each weighing. [2 marks]
(g) State two sources of error in step 4. [2 marks]
(h) State three ways in which humus improves soil for plant growth. [3 marks]
(i) Name the type of ecological factor that soil water and humus represent, and give one other example of this type of factor. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) 75.0 - 25.0 = 50.0 g
2 marks: (b)(i) 75.0 - 67.5 = 7.5 g
2 marks: (b)(ii) 7.5 / 50.0 x 100 = 15%
2 marks: (c)(i) 67.5 - 64.0 = 3.5 g
2 marks: (c)(ii) 3.5 / 50.0 x 100 = 7%
2 marks: (c)(iii) dry soil = 67.5 - 25.0 = 42.5 g; 3.5 / 42.5 x 100 = 8.2%
2 marks: (d) To make sure that all the water has been driven off
2 marks: (e) A higher temperature would burn off some organic matter (humus), giving a wrong value for water
2 marks: (f) Hot objects set up convection currents that affect the balance reading / hot soil absorbs moisture differently; weighing hot gives inaccurate mass
2 marks: (g) Any two, 1 mark each: some mineral matter (e.g. carbonates) may decompose; soil may spit out of the dish; incomplete burning of humus; moisture absorbed during cooling
3 marks: (h) Any three, 1 mark each: releases nutrients on decay; improves water-holding capacity; improves soil structure/crumb; improves aeration; supports soil organisms; buffers pH
1 mark: (i) Edaphic factors
2 marks: (i) Any one: soil pH; soil air; soil texture; soil temperature; mineral salts
questions.explanation: Fresh soil = 50.0 g; water = 7.5 g (15%); humus = 3.5 g, i.e. 7% of fresh soil or 3.5/42.5 = 8.2% of dry soil. Heating to constant mass ensures all water is removed, and keeping to 105 oC prevents burning humus. Humus supplies nutrients, holds water and improves structure. Soil water and humus are edaphic factors, like soil pH.
